claim: Reliably detecting unexpected sounds is important for environmental awareness and survival.
source: Reliably detecting unexpected sounds is important for environmental awareness and survival.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of detecting unexpected sounds, presented as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Auditory cortical neurons enhance the brain's ability to detect unexpected events through stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA) by selectively reducing responses to frequently, but not rarely, occurring sounds.
source: By selectively reducing responses to frequently, but not rarely, occurring sounds, auditory cortical neurons are thought to enhance the brain's ability to detect unexpected events through stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to existing literature and represents the theoretical framework for the study.

claim: The majority of neurons in the primary auditory cortex exhibit SSA.
source: The majority of neurons in the primary auditory cortex exhibit SSA, yet little is known about the underlying cortical circuits.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and is supported by data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1D).

claim: Two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons.
source: We found that two types of cortical interneurons differentially amplify SSA in putative excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulations.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVs) amplify SSA by providing non-specific inhibition.
source: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVs) amplify SSA by providing non-specific inhibition: optogenetic suppression of PVs led to an equal increase in responses to frequent and rare tones.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data showing equal increases in responses to both tone types upon PV suppression.

claim: Optogenetic suppression of PVs led to an equal increase in responses to frequent and rare tones.
source: Parvalbumin-positive interneurons (PVs) amplify SSA by providing non-specific inhibition: optogenetic suppression of PVs led to an equal increase in responses to frequent and rare tones.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) selectively reduce excitatory responses to frequent tones.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) selectively reduce excitatory responses to frequent tones: suppression of SOMs led to an increase in responses to frequent, but not to rare tones.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing selective effects of SOM suppression on frequent tone responses.

claim: Suppression of SOMs led to an increase in responses to frequent, but not to rare tones.
source: In contrast, somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) selectively reduce excitatory responses to frequent tones: suppression of SOMs led to an increase in responses to frequent, but not to rare tones.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: A mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory network model accounts for distinct mechanisms by which cortical inhibitory neurons enhance the brain's sensitivity to unexpected sounds.
source: A mutually coupled excitatory-inhibitory network model accounts for distinct mechanisms by which cortical inhibitory neurons enhance the brain's sensitivity to unexpected sounds.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results presented in Figure 7.

claim: Adaptation to stimulus context is thought to increase efficiency of sensory coding under the constraints of limited resources.
source: Adaptation to stimulus context is thought to increase efficiency of sensory coding under the constraints of limited resources (Barlow, 1961).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barlow, 1961, representing established theory in the field.

claim: Cortical neurons exhibit adaptation, attenuating their responses to redundant stimuli across sensory modalities.
source: Across sensory modalities, cortical neurons exhibit adaptation, attenuating their responses to redundant stimuli (Das and Gilbert, 1999; Ulanovsky et al., 2003; Garcia-Lazaro et al., 2007; Asari and Zador, 2009; Khatri et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating adaptation across different sensory systems.

claim: In the primary auditory cortex (A1), the vast majority of neurons exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA).
source: In the primary auditory cortex (A1), the vast majority of neurons exhibit stimulus-specific adaptation (SSA, Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1 and citations to previous studies.

claim: When presented with a sequence of two tones, one frequent (standard) and another rare (deviant), the neuron's response to the standard tone becomes weaker, but the response to the deviant tone remains strong.
source: When presented with a sequence of two tones, one of which occurs frequently (termed 'standard') and another rarely (termed 'deviant'), the neuron's response to the standard tone becomes weaker, but the response to the deviant tone remains strong (Ulanovsky et al., 2003; Szymanski et al., 2009; Farley et al., 2010; Fishman and Steinschneider, 2012).
evidence: This claim describes the characteristic pattern of SSA and is supported by multiple citations.

claim: SSA has been found in sub-cortical structures including the auditory midbrain and auditory thalamus.
source: Whereas SSA has also been found in sub-cortical structures e.g. in the auditory midbrain (Malmierca et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012) and the auditory thalamus (Kraus et al., 1994; Anderson et al., 2009; Antunes et al., 2010; Bauerle et al., 2011), it is weak in the lemniscal areas of the auditory pathway, which project to A1, and stronger in those non-lemniscal areas which receive feedback from A1 (Ulanovsky et al., 2004, Perez-Gonzalez et al., 2005, Duque et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies demonstrating SSA in subcortical auditory structures.

claim: SSA is weak in the lemniscal areas of the auditory pathway, which project to A1, and stronger in non-lemniscal areas which receive feedback from A1.
source: Whereas SSA has also been found in sub-cortical structures e.g. in the auditory midbrain (Malmierca et al., 2009; Zhao et al., 2011; Thomas et al., 2012) and the auditory thalamus (Kraus et al., 1994; Anderson et al., 2009; Antunes et al., 2010; Bauerle et al., 2011), it is weak in the lemniscal areas of the auditory pathway, which project to A1, and stronger in those non-lemniscal areas which receive feedback from A1 (Ulanovsky et al., 2004, Perez-Gonzalez et al., 2005, Duque et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies comparing SSA in different auditory pathway regions.

claim: Cortical circuits are proposed to contribute to and amplify SSA in A1.
source: Therefore, cortical circuits are proposed to contribute to and amplify SSA in A1 (Ulanovsky et al., 2003, Szymanski et al., 2009, Bauerle et al., 2011, Fishman and Steinschneider, 2012, Escera and Malmierca, 2014), through a combination of plastic modulation of thalamocortical inputs and intra-cortical inhibitory circuits, which would allow for selective suppression of neuronal responses to specific stimuli (Nelken, 2014).
evidence: This claim represents a hypothesis supported by multiple citations and is tested in the current study.

claim: Auditory cortex contains morphologically and physiologically diverse inhibitory interneurons, which form dense interconnected networks with excitatory neurons.
source: Auditory cortex, like other sensory cortices, contains morphologically and physiologically diverse inhibitory interneurons, which form dense interconnected networks with excitatory neurons (DeFelipe, 2002; Douglas and Martin, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing cortical interneuron diversity and connectivity.

claim: Different interneuron types have been hypothesized to carry out specialized complementary functions in sensory processing.
source: While different interneuron types have been hypothesized to carry out specialized complementary functions in sensory processing (DeFelipe, 2002; Markram et al., 2004; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Marlin et al., 2015), their function in driving changes in dynamic auditory processing has not been previously established.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations and represents the theoretical motivation for the study.

claim: The function of different interneuron types in driving changes in dynamic auditory processing has not been previously established.
source: While different interneuron types have been hypothesized to carry out specialized complementary functions in sensory processing (DeFelipe, 2002; Markram et al., 2004; Isaacson and Scanziani, 2011; Kepecs and Fishell, 2014; Marlin et al., 2015), their function in driving changes in dynamic auditory processing has not been previously established.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Parvalbumin-positive (PV) and somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons are the two most common types of interneurons in the cortex.
source: We hypothesized that the two most common types of interneurons in the cortex, parvalbumin- (PVs) and somatostatin-positive interneurons (SOMs) (Xu et al., 2010; Rudy et al., 2011), facilitate SSA in excitatory neurons of A1 in a complementary fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing interneuron populations in cortex.

claim: A subset of PVs receive direct thalamic inputs.
source: PVs, a subset of which receive direct thalamic inputs (Staiger et al., 1996), may amplify SSA in excitatory neurons by providing a constant inhibitory drive; equally strong inhibitory drive would attenuate the weak response to standard tones relatively more than the strong response to deviant tones, leading to a greater differential between standard vs deviant tone spiking response.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Staiger et al., 1996.

claim: SOMs target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells.
source: SOMs, which target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells (McGarry et al., 2010; Gentet et al., 2012), have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation (Reyes et al., 1998; Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing SOM connectivity and synaptic properties.

claim: SOMs have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation.
source: SOMs, which target distal dendrites of pyramidal cells (McGarry et al., 2010; Gentet et al., 2012), have excitatory synapses that exhibit facilitation upon repetitive stimulation (Reyes et al., 1998; Silberberg and Markram, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating synaptic facilitation at SOM synapses.

claim: Almost all neurons recorded in A1 exhibited significant SSA (138 out of 147 neurons).
source: Almost all neurons recorded in A1 exhibited significant SSA (Figure 1D, standard tone-evoked FR significantly lower than the deviant tone-evoked FR in N = 138 out of 147 neurons, Wilcoxon rank sum test p < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and reference to Figure 1D.

claim: The amplitude of current in the CSD sink reflects the strength of thalamic inputs to the cortex.
source: The amplitude of current in the sink was taken as a measure of the combined strength of post-synaptic inputs onto layer 4 neurons, which should reflect the strength of the thalamic inputs to the cortex (Metherate and Cruikshank, 1999; Kaur et al., 2005; Szymanski et al., 2009; Happel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies establishing CSD as a measure of thalamic input strength.

claim: The sink amplitude was lower for the standard as compared to the deviant tones, suggesting that excitatory signals produced by thalamo-cortical inputs exhibit SSA.
source: The sink amplitude was lower for the standard as compared to the deviant tones (Figure 1F,G), suggesting that excitatory signals produced by thalamo-cortical inputs exhibit SSA, consistent with previous findings (Szymanski et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F,G and is consistent with previous findings.

claim: The SSA index of the granular layer CSD sinks was significantly lower than that of either the non-thalamo-recipient layers or the SSA index of the mean spiking activity of A1 neurons.
source: Importantly, across sessions, the SSA index of the granular layer CSD sinks was significantly lower than that of either the non-thalamo-recipient layers (Δ = −28%, p-value from one-sided test after correction (p1) = 6e−4, z = −3.4, Bonferroni corrected for two tests (C = 2)) or the SSA index of the mean spiking activity of A1 neurons (Δ = 23%, p1 = 0.029, z = −2.1, C = 2) in each session (N = 20 sessions in 15 mice, Figure 1G), suggesting that additional intra-cortical mechanisms may contribute to SSA in the cortex.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data comparing SSA indices across cortical layers.

claim: Additional intra-cortical mechanisms may contribute to SSA in the cortex.
source: Importantly, across sessions, the SSA index of the granular layer CSD sinks was significantly lower than that of either the non-thalamo-recipient layers (Δ = −28%, p-value from one-sided test after correction (p1) = 6e−4, z = −3.4, Bonferroni corrected for two tests (C = 2)) or the SSA index of the mean spiking activity of A1 neurons (Δ = 23%, p1 = 0.029, z = −2.1, C = 2) in each session (N = 20 sessions in 15 mice, Figure 1G), suggesting that additional intra-cortical mechanisms may contribute to SSA in the cortex.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that SSA is stronger in spiking activity than in thalamic inputs.

claim: Arch was expressed selectively in PVs or SOMs in auditory cortex at expected levels.
source: 2 weeks following virus injection, Arch was expressed selectively in PVs or SOMs in auditory cortex at expected levels (Kvitsiani et al., 2013) (Figure 2B,C PV-Cre: N = 250 neurons in 4 mice, specificity = 92 ± 1%, efficiency = 73 ± 5%. SOM-Cre: N = 149 neurons in 5 mice, specificity = 95 ± 2%, efficiency = 86 ± 5%).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2B,C and quantification of expression efficiency and specificity.

claim: Light cast over A1 drives a strong suppressive current and hyperpolarizes the membrane potential in PVs and SOMs in vitro.
source: In vitro intracellular recordings from optically identified PVs or SOMs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) demonstrate that light cast over the auditory cortex in vitro drives a strong suppressive current (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplements 1C,D, 2C,D) and hyperpolarizes the membrane potential in these neurons (Figure 2—figure supplements 1B, 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2 and supplementary figures.

claim: Illuminating the auditory cortex suppressed spiking activity in a small subset of recorded neurons (putative inhibitory neurons) and increased activity in a great majority of recorded neurons (putative excitatory neurons) in vivo.
source: In vivo, in both PV-Cre and SOM-Cre mice, illuminating the auditory cortex suppressed spiking activity in a small subset of recorded neurons (Figure 2E,F, left, putative inhibitory neurons) and increased activity in a great majority of recorded neurons (Figure 2E,F right, putative excitatory neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo electrophysiology data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Shining light over A1 increased spontaneous neuronal activity in the majority of the recorded neurons in both PV-Cre mice (102 out of 115 neurons) and SOM-Cre mice (61 out of 104 neurons).
source: Shining light over A1 increased spontaneous neuronal activity in the majority of the recorded neurons in both PV-Cre mice (N = 115 neurons, 102 increased, 0 decreased, in 10 mice) (Figure 2G) and SOM-Cre mice (N = 104 neurons, 61 increased, 3 decreased, in 9 mice) (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantification of light effects on spontaneous activity shown in Figure 2G,H.

claim: Photosuppression of either PVs or SOMs resulted in a significant reduction in SSA index across the population.
source: Photosuppression of either PVs or SOMs affected the responses of neurons to the tones (Figure 3B,C), resulting in a significant reduction in SSA index across the population (Figure 3E,F, PV-Cre: Δ = −41%, p1 = 1e−12, t(66) = 8.6. SOM-Cre: Δ = −25%, p1 = 2e−6, t(42) = 5.4).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of SSA indices with and without photosuppression, shown in Figure 3E,F.

claim: In a control group of PV-Cre or SOM-Cre mice injected with fluorescent reporter alone, SSA was not affected by light.
source: In a control group of PV-Cre or SOM-Cre mice (6 mice), we injected a modified AAV, which encoded anti-sense fluorescent reporter alone under the FLEX cassette, and computed the effect of casting light on SSA (SSA was found in 33 out of 37 tone-responsive neurons in control mice). In this control group, SSA was not affected by light (Figure 3D,G, p > 0.05, t(36) = −2.0), confirming that Arch expression was required for the effect of the light.
evidence: This claim is supported by control experiments shown in Figure 3D,G demonstrating that Arch expression is necessary for the observed effects.

claim: Both types of interneurons contribute to the reduction of the response of the neuron to the stimulus during SSA.
source: These results demonstrate that both types of interneurons contribute to the reduction of the response of the neuron to the stimulus during SSA.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the observation that suppressing either PV or SOM reduces SSA.

claim: Suppressing PVs led to increased FR to both the standard (Δ = 102%) and deviant (Δ = 56%) tones.
source: In addition to increasing spontaneous activity (Δ = 185%, p-value from one-sided t-test after correction (p2) = 3e−11, t(159) = −7.2), suppressing PVs led to increased FR to both the standard (Δ = 102%, p2 = 3e−11, t(159) = −7.2) and deviant (Δ = 56%, p2 = 9e−12, t(159) = −7.4) tones (N = 160, Figure 4A–C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate changes upon PV suppression, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The difference in FR due to suppression of PVs was not significantly different between the standard and deviant tones.
source: The difference in FR due to suppression of PVs was not significantly different between the standard and deviant tones (p2 > 0.05, t(159) = −0.1, C = 2) but both were greater than the difference in the spontaneous FR (standard: Δ = 25%, p2 = 0.001, t(159) = −3.6, C = 2. Deviant: Δ = 26%, p2 = 0.039, t(159) = −2.4, C = 2), indicating that the change in tone-evoked FR was similar regardless of tone probability (Figure 4B, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of firing rate changes for standard vs. deviant tones.

claim: Suppression of SOMs led to an increase in FR for spontaneous activity (Δ = 46%) and during the standard (Δ = 29%) but not deviant tone.
source: By contrast, suppressing SOMs led to an increase in FR for spontaneous activity (Δ = 46%, p2 = 2e−9, t(113) = −6.5) and during the standard (Δ = 29%, p2 = 2e−8, t(113) = −6.1) but not deviant (p2 > 0.05, t(113) = −0.8) tone (N = 114, Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of firing rate changes upon SOM suppression, shown in Figure 4.

claim: The increase in FR for spontaneous activity was not different than that during the standard tone upon SOM suppression.
source: The increase in FR for spontaneous activity was not different than that during the standard tone (p2 > 0.05, t(113) = 0.2, C = 2) and the differences in FR due to suppression of SOMs were stronger for spontaneous activity and the standard tone than the deviant tone (spontaneous: Δ = 390%, p2 = 0.004, t(113) = 3.1. Standard: Δ = 378%, p2 = 0.005, t(113) = 3.1) (Figure 4E, bottom panel), thereby accounting for the change in SSA with SOM inactivation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of firing rate changes across conditions.

claim: The effect of PVs on SSA was equally strong in the supra-granular and infra-granular layers, but stronger in the granular layer.
source: The effect of PVs on SSA was equally strong in the supra-granular and infra-granular layers, but stronger in the granular layer, that is, the thalamo-recipient layer. This differential effect is consistent with the relative proportion of cortical interneurons that are PVs, which is higher in granular than either in infra- or supra-granular layers (Lee et al., 2010; Xu et al., 2010; Ouellet and de Villers-Sidani, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar analysis of SSA effects shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and is consistent with known PV distributions.

claim: Suppressing SOMs reduced SSA in the granular and infra-granular layers but did not have a significant effect on SSA in the supra-granular layers.
source: In contrast, suppressing SOMs reduced SSA in the granular (N = 7, Δ = −42%, p2 = 0.031) and infra-granular (N = 63, Δ = −24%, p2 = 6e−7, z = 5.0) layers but did not have a significant effect on SSA in the supra-granular layers (N = 3, p2 > 0.05) (B, center).
evidence: This claim is supported by laminar analysis of SSA effects shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both PVs and SOMs exhibited SSA, evidenced by a significant reduction in standard tone-evoked FR compared to the deviant tone response.
source: Both PVs and SOMs exhibited SSA, evidenced by a significant reduction in standard tone-evoked FR compared to the deviant tone response (Figure 6B,C,E,F, PV: N = 16, Δ = −32%, p2 = 0.023, z = −2.5, C = 2. SOM: N = 28, Δ = −41%, p2 = 0.002, z = −3.3, C = 2. Signed-rank test).
evidence: This claim is supported by optogenetic identification and recording of PV and SOM responses shown in Figure 6.

claim: The SSA index was not significantly different between PVs and SOMs.
source: The SSA index was not significantly different between PVs and SOMs (Figure 6G, neurons responsive to both tones A and B—PV: N = 5, SOM: N = 12. PV and SOM: p2 > 0.05, C = 2. Rank sum test) and both were similar to the mean SSA index in putative excitatory neurons (Figure 6G—Exc: N = 67. Exc vs PV: p > 0.05, z = 0.7, C = 2. Exc vs SOM: p > 0.05, z = 0.4, C = 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical comparison of SSA indices across cell types shown in Figure 6G.

claim: PVs' response to the equal tones did not decrease significantly as compared to deviant tones, whereas SOMs adapted in their response to equal tones.
source: PVs and SOMs exhibited some differences in relative response changes between the deviant, the standard, and the equal tones (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2B,D); PVs' response to the equal tones did not decrease significantly as compared to deviant tones (N = 16 p2 > 0.05, z = −1.7, C = 2), whereas SOMs adapted in their response to equal tones (Δ = −36%, p2 = 0.049, z = −2.3, C = 2), and then further to standard tones (N = 28, Δ = −49%, p2 = 0.022, z = −2.6, C = 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of responses to equal probability tones shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: SOMs may adapt at a faster time scale than PVs with repeated presentation of tones.
source: These results suggest that SOMs may adapt at a faster time scale than PVs with repeated presentation of tones.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the differential adaptation patterns observed for PVs and SOMs.

claim: The model replicated the differential effects of manipulation of PV and SOM activity on responses to standard and deviant tones in putative excitatory neurons.
source: The model replicated the differential effects of manipulation of PV and SOM activity on responses to standard and deviant tones in putative excitatory neurons (Figure 7B–E): when PVs were suppressed optogenetically, the responses to both the standard and the deviant tones increased (Figure 7B,C). By contrast, when SOMs were suppressed, although the spontaneous FR and standard tone-evoked FR were elevated, the responses to the deviant tone remained constant, whereas the responses to the standard tone increased (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: Including inhibition between SOMs and PVs did not affect the model outcome.
source: SOMs have been shown to inhibit PVs (Cottam et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013; Sturgill and Isaacson, 2015). Including inhibition between SOMs and PVs did not affect the model outcome, with suppression of PVs resulting in suppression of excitatory responses to both the standard and the deviant, and suppression of SOMs driving specific suppression of excitatory responses to the standard, but not the deviant (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by additional modeling results shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and citations to studies showing SOM-to-PV inhibition.

claim: The observed differential effects of PV and SOM suppression may be due to their differential action on excitatory neuronal responses in the unadapted and adapted state.
source: Our model provides an intuition for this effect: the mutually coupled excitatory–inhibitory network model demonstrates that the observed differential effects of PV and SOM suppression may be due to their differential action on excitatory neuronal responses in the unadapted and adapted state (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from the computational model results shown in Figure 7.

claim: SSA may serve an additional function: to adjust the responses of neurons in a range that is more sensitive to small changes in the inputs from both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
source: Thus, SSA may serve an additional function: to adjust the responses of neurons in a range that is more sensitive to small changes in the inputs from both excitatory and inhibitory neuronal populations.
evidence: This claim is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: A circuit element, such as PVs or SOMs, that itself adapts may further amplify adaptation in the excitatory neurons.
source: More generally, the simulation demonstrates that a circuit element, such as PVs or SOMs, that itself adapts may further amplify adaptation in the excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim is a general principle derived from the modeling results.

claim: The findings expand on the 'adaptation in narrowly tuned units' model, which proposes that repeated presentation of the standard stimulus drives adaptation within more narrowly tuned inputs, such as thalamocortical inputs.
source: This series of findings expands on the 'adaptation in narrowly tuned units' model, which proposes that repeated presentation of the standard stimulus drives adaptation within more narrowly tuned inputs, such as thalamocortical inputs (Mill et al., 2011; Taaseh et al., 2011; Nelken, 2014).
evidence: This claim places the current findings in the context of existing theoretical models, supported by citations.

claim: PVs contribute to SSA by providing a constant level of inhibition, resulting in a relatively higher inhibitory drive during the presentation of the standard, as compared to the deviant.
source: Our data indicate dual effects of cortical inhibition on SSA: (1) PVs contribute to SSA by providing a constant level of inhibition, resulting in a relatively higher inhibitory drive during the presentation of the standard, as compared to the deviant.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the experimental data on PV function in SSA.

claim: The constant inhibition from PVs amplifies the effect of thalamocortical depression in suppressing the response of the neuron to repeated stimulus.
source: Taking into account the non-linear synaptic input to FR output function of a typical pyramidal neuron, the constant inhibition amplifies the effect of thalamocortical depression in suppressing the response of the neuron to repeated stimulus (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the modeling results and known properties of pyramidal neurons.

claim: The selective increase of the inhibitory drive from SOMs for standard stimulus as compared to the deviant stimulus responses might be explained by a shift in the non-linear transfer function between inputs to SOMs and their outputs to excitatory neurons, possibly due to facilitation of SOM-to-excitatory neuron synapses.
source: The selective increase of the inhibitory drive from SOMs for standard stimulus as compared to the deviant stimulus responses might be explained by a shift in the non-linear transfer function between inputs to SOMs and their outputs to excitatory neurons, possibly due to facilitation of SOM-to-excitatory neuron synapses (Beierlein et al., 2003; Silberberg and Markram, 2007) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is a mechanistic interpretation supported by modeling results and citations to studies on synaptic facilitation.

claim: Thalamocortical synapses onto inhibitory neurons and synapses from inhibitory neurons to excitatory cells can be depressing.
source: This finding is consistent with previous results that found that thalamocortical synapses onto inhibitory neurons and synapses from inhibitory neurons to excitatory cells can be depressing (Tan et al., 2008; Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies demonstrating synaptic depression.

claim: SSA has been linked to detection of deviant sounds.
source: While not demonstrated directly, SSA has been linked to detection of deviant sounds (Ulanovsky et al., 2003), which may be facilitated by a relatively enhanced neuronal response to a change in the ongoing sound (Nelken et al., 2003; Winkler et al., 2009; Grimm and Escera, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies linking SSA to deviant detection, though the authors note it has not been directly demonstrated.

claim: Whether and how modulating SSA in the auditory cortex affects auditory behavior has not yet been tested.
source: However, whether and how modulating SSA in the auditory cortex affects auditory behavior has not yet been tested.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in knowledge and suggests future research directions.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons may prove to have a complementary role in shaping auditory perception in addition to receptive field reorganization driven by synaptic plasticity.
source: Inhibitory interneurons may prove to have a complementary role in shaping auditory perception in addition to receptive field reorganization driven by synaptic plasticity (Froemke et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is a speculative statement about the potential role of interneurons, supported by a citation.

claim: The use of optogenetic methods to test the function of inhibitory interneurons in SSA overcomes the limitations of lesion or pharmacological studies.
source: The use of optogenetic methods to test the function of inhibitory interneurons in SSA overcomes the limitations of lesion or pharmacological studies (Elliott and Trahiotis, 1972; Duque et al., 2014), which only allow for prolonged, non-selective inactivation (Moore et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating limitations of alternative methods.

claim: All experiments were performed in adult male mice aged 12–15 weeks and weighing 22–32 g.
source: All experiments were performed in adult male mice (Jackson Laboratories, Bar Harbor, ME, United States; age, 12–15 weeks; weight, 22–32 g; PV-Cre mice, strain: B6;129P2-Pvalbtm1(cre)Arbr/J; SOM-Cre: Ssttm2.1(cre)Zjh/J) housed at 28°C on a 12-hr light:dark cycle with water and food provided ad libitum.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the experimental subjects.

claim: In PV-Cre mice, Cre recombinase is expressed in parvalbumin-positive interneurons; in SOM-Cre mice, Cre is expressed in somatostatin-positive interneurons.
source: In PV-Cre mice, Cre recombinase (Cre) is expressed in parvalbumin-positive interneurons; in SOM-Cre mice, Cre is expressed in somatostatin-positive interneurons (Taniguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim describes the genetic tools used in the study, supported by a citation.

claim: Modified AAV encoding Arch under FLEX promoter was used for selective suppression of PVs or SOMs.
source: Modified AAV encoding Arch under FLEX promoter was used for selective suppression of PVs or SOMs (catalog number AV-9-PV2432, AAV9.CBA.Flex.Arch-GFP.WPRE.SV40, Addgene22222, serotype 2/9) (Chow et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the viral vectors used, supported by a citation.

claim: Modified AAV encoding ChR2 under FLEX promoter was used for selective excitation of PVs or SOMs.
source: Modified AAV encoding ChR2 under FLEX promoter was used for selective excitation of PVs or SOMs (catalog number AV-9-18917P, AAV9.CAGGS.Flex.ChR2-tdTomato.WPRE.SV40, Addgene18917, serotype 2/9).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the viral vectors used for optogenetic activation.

claim: A 750 nl bolus of AAV in water was injected into A1 (1 mm ventral from pia mater) 2–3 weeks prior to the start of experimental recordings.
source: 2–3 weeks prior to the start of experimental recordings, a 0.5-mm diameter craniotomy was drilled over primary auditory cortex (2.6 mm caudal and 4.1 mm lateral from bregma) under aseptic conditions while the mouse was anesthetized with isoflurane. A 750 nl bolus of AAV in water was injected into A1 (1 mm ventral from pia mater) using a stereotaxic syringe pump (Pump 11 Elite Nanomite, Havard Apparatus, Holliston, MA, United States).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the virus injection procedure.

claim: Electrodes were targeted to A1 on the basis of stereotaxic coordinates and in relation to blood vessels.
source: Electrodes were targeted to A1 on the basis of stereotaxic coordinates and in relation to blood vessels.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing electrode targeting.

claim: The location was confirmed by examining the click and tone-pip responses of the recorded units for characteristic responses of neurons in core auditory areas.
source: In electrophysiological recordings, the location was confirmed by examining the click and tone-pip responses of the recorded units for characteristic responses of neurons in core auditory areas, as described previously by our group in the rat (Carruthers et al., 2013) and by other groups in the mouse (Linden and Schreiner, 2003; Guo et al., 2012; Marlin et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing how recording location was verified, supported by citations.

claim: While the electrodes were targeted to A1, some recordings may include data from the anterior auditory field, adjacent to A1.
source: While the electrodes were targeted to A1, some recordings may include data from the anterior auditory field, adjacent to A1 (Linden et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a potential limitation in the recording location specificity.

claim: Raw signals from 32 channels were bandpass filtered at 600–6000 Hz and thresholded for spike analysis, or at 10–300 Hz for LFP and CSD analysis.
source: Raw signals from 32 channels were bandpass filtered at 600–6000 Hz and thresholded for spike analysis, or at 10–300 Hz for LFP and CSD analysis (Poly-2 probe only), digitized at 32 kHz and stored for offline analysis (Neuralynx, Bozeman, MT, United States).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing signal processing procedures.

claim: Spike sorting was performed using commercial software (Offline Sorter, Plexon, Dallas, TX, United States).
source: Spike sorting was performed using commercial software (Offline Sorter, Plexon, Dallas, TX, United States) (Carruthers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the spike sorting procedure.

claim: A stringent set of criteria was used to isolate single units from multiunit clusters.
source: We used a stringent set of criteria to isolate single units from multiunit clusters (Otazu et al., 2009; Bizley et al., 2010; Brasselet et al., 2012; Durand et al., 2012; Carruthers et al., 2013; Picard et al., 2014; Carruthers et al., 2015). Single-unit clusters contained <1% of spikes within a 1.0-ms interspike interval, and the spike waveforms across 3 or 4 channels had to form a visually identifiable distinct cluster in a projection onto a three-dimensional subspace.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing unit isolation criteria, supported by citations.

claim: Putative excitatory neurons were identified based on their expected response patterns to sounds and the lack of significant suppression of the spontaneous FR due to light.
source: Putative excitatory neurons were identified based on their expected response patterns to sounds and the lack of significant suppression of the spontaneous FR due to light (Lima et al., 2009; Moore and Wehr, 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing neuron classification, supported by citations.

claim: Only 2% of all recorded neurons were significantly photosuppressed at baseline.
source: While this subpopulation may still contain inhibitory neurons, only 2% of all recorded neurons were significantly photosuppressed at baseline (one-sided paired t-test, significance taken at p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a quantification of the proportion of neurons showing photosuppression, supporting the classification method.

claim: Speakers were calibrated prior to the experiments to ±3 dB over frequencies between 1 and 40 kHz.
source: Speakers were calibrated prior to the experiments to ±3 dB over frequencies between 1 and 40 kHz, by placing a microphone (Brüel and Kjaer, Denmark) in the location of the ear contralateral to the recorded A1 hemisphere, recording speaker output and filtering stimuli to compensate for acoustic aberrations (Carruthers et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing acoustic calibration procedures.

claim: Two frequencies (separated by 0.39 octaves), which elicited spiking responses of similar strength, were selected as tone A and B.
source: Frequency response functions were calculated online for several multiunits, and two frequencies (separated by 0.39 octaves), which elicited spiking responses of similar strength, were selected as tone A and B.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing stimulus selection.

claim: Each oddball stimulus consisted of a train of 653 A and B tones (100-ms long, 300-ms ISI, 65-dB SPL).
source: Next, a series of stimuli composed of tones A and B were presented in interleaved blocks, repeated four times. Each oddball stimulus consisted of a train of 653 A and B tones (100-ms long, 300-ms ISI, 65-dB SPL).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the oddball stimulus parameters.

claim: A frozen sequence of standard and deviant tones in pseudorandom order was used and counterbalanced with respect to the number of standard tones preceding each deviant.
source: We used a frozen sequence of standard and deviant tones in pseudorandom order and counterbalanced with respect to the number of standard tones preceding each deviant.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the stimulus sequence design.

claim: During every fifth tone of the oddball and equal probability stimuli, light was cast over A1 to suppress interneurons.
source: During every fifth tone of the oddball and equal probability stimuli, light was cast over A1 to suppress interneurons. The light onset was 100 ms prior to tone onset, and lasted for 250 ms.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the optogenetic manipulation protocol.

claim: At 180 mW/mm2, light pulses were intense enough to significantly modulate multiunit activity throughout all cortical layers.
source: At 180 mW/mm2, light pulses were intense enough to significantly modulate multiunit activity throughout all cortical layers.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the light intensity used and its effectiveness.

claim: The effect of optical stimulation was not significant for responses to subsequent tones.
source: The effect of optical stimulation was not significant for responses to subsequent tones (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurons were identified as PVs or SOMs if they responded to brief (5 ms) flashes of light with spikes within 1.5–4.5 ms of laser pulse onset.
source: Neurons were identified as PVs or SOMs if they responded to brief (5 ms) flashes of light with spikes within 1.5–4.5 ms of laser pulse onset (Figure 6A,D).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the optogenetic identification criteria.

claim: For each putative excitatory neuron, the spontaneous FR and tone-evoked FRs were measured as the mean FR over 50 ms pre- and post-tone onset, respectively.
source: For each putative excitatory neuron, the spontaneous FR and tone-evoked FRs were measured as the mean FR over 50 ms pre- and post-tone onset, respectively.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing firing rate measurement.

claim: For each identified interneuron, FRs were measured 100 ms pre- and post-tone onset.
source: For each identified interneuron, FRs were measured 100 ms pre- and post-tone onset.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing firing rate measurement for interneurons.

claim: To calculate the CSD, the net current density moving through cortical tissue at 32 positions along the cortical axis was calculated based on LFPs of responses to tones recorded on each electrode, by using the second order central finite difference to calculate the second spatial derivative across the LFPs over the vertically arranged electrodes.
source: To calculate the CSD, the net current density moving through cortical tissue at 32 positions along the cortical axis was calculated based on LFPs of responses to tones recorded on each electrode, by using the second order central finite difference to calculate the second spatial derivative across the LFPs over the vertically arranged electrodes (Szymanski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing CSD calculation, supported by a citation.

claim: Across the CSD profile, the deepest current sink corresponds to the thalamo-recipient granular layer.
source: Across the CSD profile, the deepest current sink corresponds to the thalamo-recipient granular layer (Kaur et al., 2005; Szymanski et al., 2009) allowing us to reconstruct the laminar location of recorded neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies establishing this relationship.

claim: The parameters of the excitatory-inhibitory network model were chosen in order to achieve a match to experimental data.
source: We constructed firing-rate models based on Wilson–Cowan dynamics (Staiger et al., 1996; Xu et al., 2010, Rudy et al., 2011). The parameters were chosen in order to achieve a match to experimental data.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the modeling approach.
